questions.prompt: A whole is split into four equal parts. One part is…
questions.explanation: Quarter is the name for one of four equal parts.

questions.prompt: A sandwich is cut into one big piece and one small piece. Are both halves?
questions.explanation: Two pieces count as halves only when they are equal shares of the whole.

questions.prompt: For the same whole, which single part is larger?
options: There is no way to compare
questions.explanation: Splitting into two gives larger pieces than splitting the same whole into eight.

title: Fractions start with equal pieces
practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.html:
You and a friend share a rectangular sandwich. A cut down the middle can give each of you an equal amount. Each share is one half of the sandwich.

Now imagine a cut very close to one edge. There are still two pieces, but one is much larger. Calling either piece “a half” would hide that difference. Fractions such as halves and quarters describe equal parts of a chosen whole.
sections.title: One sandwich, two people

sections.html:
Draw two identical strips. Divide the first into two equal parts and the second into eight. Shade one part of each strip and compare their sizes.

Look at one piece when there are two parts, then one piece when there are eight. More equal parts mean each individual part is smaller, as long as the whole stays the same size.

One of four equal pieces is called one quarter. The pieces must be equal: a tiny corner and a huge leftover piece would not be two equal shares.
sections.title: Try it yourself

sections.html:
Half a small sandwich and half a large sandwich are both halves, but they may contain different amounts of food. “A half” describes a relationship to a whole, not a fixed size by itself.

In the activities in this course, comparison strips have the same length. That makes comparing their shaded fractions fair. If the wholes changed size without warning, the picture could be misleading.
sections.title: Always name the whole

sections.html:
Fold a strip of paper into two equal sections, then fold it again to make four. Unfold it and check the sections. Two of the four sections cover the same length as one of the two original sections.

Do not worry about the written fraction yet. First get comfortable describing the picture: how many equal parts make the whole, and how many of those parts are selected? The next lesson gives those two counts their names.

For the full picture, explore seven friendly starting points for basic arithmetic.
sections.title: Make your own example

description: A half needs two equal shares. Learn why cutting something into two pieces is not always the same as halving it.
